items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “activities that extract raw materials from the land or sea, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining”.
items.answer: Primary sector
items.markingKey: Primary sector: activities that extract raw materials from the land or sea, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining. [1]

items.stem: Explain the changes in employment structure shown by the Clark-Fisher model.
items.answer: Pre-industrial: most work in the primary sector; industrialisation: mechanisation of farming releases labour to manufacturing, secondary share rises; post-industrial: automation and global shift reduce manufacturing, rising incomes increase demand for services.

items.stem: Explain why employment in the primary sector falls as countries develop.
items.answer: Mechanisation and higher productivity in farming; better jobs and pay in cities attract workers; declining share of income spent on food.

items.stem: Table 26.1 shows employment structure (% of workers in primary, secondary and tertiary sectors) for Country B: 1970: 51%, 15%, 34%; 1990: 30%, 27%, 43%; 2010: 15%, 28%, 57%; 2025: 3%, 30%, 67%. Suggest why the tertiary sector grew.
items.answer: Rising incomes increase demand for services (retail, health, education, finance, tourism); government services expand; ICT and outsourcing; automation reduces manufacturing jobs.

items.stem: Table 26.1 shows employment structure (% of workers in primary, secondary and tertiary sectors) for Country B: 1970: 57%, 10%, 33%; 1990: 45%, 15%, 40%; 2010: 28%, 12%, 60%; 2025: 11%, 12%, 77%. (a) Identify the year in which the secondary sector share was highest. (b) Suggest reasons for the fall in primary employment.
items.answer: (a) 1990 (15%) (b) Mechanisation and higher farm productivity; rural-urban migration for better-paid jobs; land consolidation; decline of mining.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that the Clark-Fisher model is no longer useful for understanding economic development. In your answer you may refer to globalisation, deindustrialisation and NICs.
items.answer: For: Globalisation, the global shift and the growth of informal services mean countries no longer follow the HIC path; service-led growth (India) and premature deindustrialisation. Against: The general trend from primary to secondary to tertiary still applies (South Korea, China); it is a useful descriptive framework for comparing countries. Conclusion: The model describes broad trends, but paths of development are now more varied.

options: Activities that process raw materials and manufacture goods.
Activities that extract raw materials from the land or sea, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining.

Activities that provide services, such as retail, transport, health and education.

items.stem: Explain the limitations of the Clark-Fisher model.
items.answer: Based on the historical experience of HICs; ignores the informal sector; globalisation lets countries specialise differently; some LICs have large informal tertiary sectors without industrialisation.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a UN composite measure of development combining life expectancy, education (mean and expected years of schooling) and GNI per capita (PPP)”.
items.answer: Human Development Index (HDI)
items.markingKey: Human Development Index (HDI): a UN composite measure of development combining life expectancy, education (mean and expected years of schooling) and GNI per capita (PPP). [1]

items.stem: Explain why the HDI is a better measure of development than GNI per capita alone.
items.answer: It includes health and education as well as income, reflecting quality of life; two countries with similar incomes may differ greatly in life expectancy and schooling.

items.stem: Explain the limitations of the HDI.
items.answer: Averages hide inequality within countries; omits political freedom, environment and gender inequality; data quality varies; equal weighting is arbitrary; slow to change.

items.stem: Country X has a life expectancy of 70.7 years, mean years of schooling of 10.6, expected years of schooling of 14.8 and GNI per capita of US$2 500 (PPP). Health index = (LE − 20) ÷ 65. Education index = (mean years ÷ 15 + expected years ÷ 18) ÷ 2. Income index = (ln GNI − ln 100) ÷ (ln 75 000 − ln 100). HDI = cube root of (health × education × income). Suggest why the HDI may not reflect the well-being of all people in Country X.
items.answer: It is an average and hides inequality by income, region, gender and ethnicity; it omits freedom, security and environmental quality.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that the development gap is widening. In your answer you may refer to NICs and fragile states.
items.answer: For: The gap in absolute income between the richest and poorest countries has grown; some LDCs and fragile states have stagnated; inequality within countries is rising. Conclusion: The gap has narrowed for many countries and indicators, but widened for the poorest and most fragile states.

items.stem: Explain the reasons for the rapid growth of NICs.
items.answer: Export-oriented policies; investment in education and skills; low labour costs at first; strong state planning, credit and protection for key industries; FDI; high savings; location on trade routes; Cold War aid.

items.stem: Explain the problems that may result from rapid economic growth in emerging economies.
items.answer: Pollution and environmental damage; regional inequality; rapid urbanisation and slums; rising income inequality; exploitation of workers; dependence on exports and FDI.

(b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Manufacturing output can rise while manufacturing employment falls.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. It plots sectoral shares through stages of development. (b) Correct. Automation raises productivity.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A revision website states: “The model shows employment by sector over time.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “A large tertiary sector always indicates a high level of development.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. It plots sectoral shares through stages of development. (b) Not correct. Many LICs have large informal service sectors.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 26.1 shows employment structure (% of workers in primary, secondary and tertiary sectors) for Country B: 1970: 54%, 17%, 29%; 1990: 37%, 25%, 38%; 2010: 16%, 27%, 57%; 2025: 3%, 25%, 72%. Calculate the change in the share of primary employment between 1970 and 2025, in percentage points and as a percentage change.
items.answer: −51 percentage points; −94.4%

items.stem: Table 26.1 shows employment structure (% of workers in primary, secondary and tertiary sectors) for Country B: 1970: 61%, 20%, 19%; 1990: 47%, 27%, 26%; 2010: 30%, 26%, 44%; 2025: 12%, 24%, 64%. Suggest why the tertiary sector grew.
items.answer: Rising incomes increase demand for services (retail, health, education, finance, tourism); government services expand; ICT and outsourcing; automation reduces manufacturing jobs.

items.stem: Table 26.1 shows employment structure (% of workers in primary, secondary and tertiary sectors) for Country A: 1970: 65%, 17%, 18%; 1990: 52%, 22%, 26%; 2010: 34%, 21%, 45%; 2025: 18%, 16%, 66%. (a) Identify the year in which the secondary sector share was highest. (b) Suggest why the tertiary sector grew.
items.answer: (a) 1990 (22%) (b) Rising incomes increase demand for services (retail, health, education, finance, tourism); government services expand; ICT and outsourcing; automation reduces manufacturing jobs.

items.stem: Table 26.1 shows employment structure (% of workers in primary, secondary and tertiary sectors) for Country A: 1970: 59%, 19%, 22%; 1990: 41%, 28%, 31%; 2010: 25%, 23%, 52%; 2025: 7%, 22%, 71%. (a) Calculate the change in the share of primary employment between 1970 and 2025, in percentage points and as a percentage change. (b) Describe how the changes fit the Clark-Fisher model.
items.answer: (a) −52 percentage points; −88.1% (b) Primary employment falls steadily; secondary rises with industrialisation and then falls; tertiary grows to become the largest sector, as the model predicts.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a measure of inequality from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has everything)”.
items.answer: Gini coefficient
items.markingKey: Gini coefficient: a measure of inequality from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has everything). [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A student writes: “The HDI measures inequality within a country.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why the HDI is a better measure of development than GNI per capita alone.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. The inequality-adjusted IHDI does this; the standard HDI uses averages. (b) It includes health and education as well as income, reflecting quality of life; two countries with similar incomes may differ greatly in life expectancy and schooling.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the HDI is a better measure of development than GNI per capita alone. (b) Explain the limitations of the HDI.
items.answer: (a) It includes health and education as well as income, reflecting quality of life; two countries with similar incomes may differ greatly in life expectancy and schooling. (b) Averages hide inequality within countries; omits political freedom, environment and gender inequality; data quality varies; equal weighting is arbitrary; slow to change.

items.stem: Country X has a life expectancy of 68.4 years, mean years of schooling of 6.9, expected years of schooling of 10.5 and GNI per capita of US$15 000 (PPP). Health index = (LE − 20) ÷ 65. Education index = (mean years ÷ 15 + expected years ÷ 18) ÷ 2. Income index = (ln GNI − ln 100) ÷ (ln 75 000 − ln 100). HDI = cube root of (health × education × income). Explain why a logarithm of income is used in the HDI.
items.answer: Each extra dollar adds less to well-being at higher incomes (diminishing returns), so the log reduces the influence of very high incomes.

items.stem: Country X has a life expectancy of 76.7 years, mean years of schooling of 4, expected years of schooling of 6.2 and GNI per capita of US$9 000 (PPP). Health index = (LE − 20) ÷ 65. Education index = (mean years ÷ 15 + expected years ÷ 18) ÷ 2. Income index = (ln GNI − ln 100) ÷ (ln 75 000 − ln 100). HDI = cube root of (health × education × income). Suggest why the HDI may not reflect the well-being of all people in Country X.
items.answer: It is an average and hides inequality by income, region, gender and ethnicity; it omits freedom, security and environmental quality.

items.stem: Country X has a life expectancy of 56 years, mean years of schooling of 7.3, expected years of schooling of 10.6 and GNI per capita of US$9 000 (PPP). Health index = (LE − 20) ÷ 65. Education index = (mean years ÷ 15 + expected years ÷ 18) ÷ 2. Income index = (ln GNI − ln 100) ÷ (ln 75 000 − ln 100). HDI = cube root of (health × education × income). (a) Calculate the health and education indices. (b) Calculate the income index.
items.answer: (a) health 0.554; education 0.538 (b) 0.68

items.stem: “The development gap is widening.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to NICs, income and fragile states.
items.answer: For: The gap in absolute income between the richest and poorest countries has grown; some LDCs and fragile states have stagnated; inequality within countries is rising. Against: Many countries, especially in Asia, have converged; global poverty fell sharply until 2019; HDI gaps in life expectancy and schooling have narrowed. Conclusion: The gap has narrowed for many countries and indicators, but widened for the poorest and most fragile states.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “emerging economy”?
options: A large family-controlled business conglomerate in South Korea, such as Samsung or Hyundai.
A grouping of major emerging economies, originally Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, expanded from 2024.
A country with rapid economic growth and increasing integration into global markets, such as China, India, Brazil, Indonesia and Mexico.
The first-generation NICs: South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore.
items.answer: A country with rapid economic growth and increasing integration into global markets, such as China, India, Brazil, Indonesia and Mexico.
items.markingKey: Emerging economy: a country with rapid economic growth and increasing integration into global markets, such as China, India, Brazil, Indonesia and Mexico. [1]

items.stem: A revision website states: “NICs no longer have any low-wage industries.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many still have low-wage sectors and informal employment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why some NICs have moved into high-technology industries. (b) Explain the reasons for the rapid growth of NICs.
items.answer: (a) Rising wages reduced competitiveness in labour-intensive industry; investment in R&D and universities; government strategy; skilled workforce; brands such as Samsung and TSMC. (b) Export-oriented policies; investment in education and skills; low labour costs at first; strong state planning, credit and protection for key industries; FDI; high savings; location on trade routes; Cold War aid.

items.stem: Country P, an emerging economy, had GDP per capita (constant US$) of 800 in 1990 and 1 990 in 2020. Calculate the mean annual growth rate.
items.answer: 3.08% per year

items.stem: Country P, an emerging economy, had GDP per capita (constant US$) of 800 in 2000 and 2 820 in 2025. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in GDP per capita over the period. (b) Use the rule of 70 to estimate how long it took GDP per capita to double.
items.answer: (a) +252.5% (b) about 13.5 years

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the growth of NICs and emerging economies has been driven mainly by globalisation? In your answer you may refer to education and state policy.
items.answer: For: FDI, TNC outsourcing, access to global markets and global value chains (Vietnam, China, Mexico) drove growth. Against: Domestic factors were decisive: state planning, land reform, education, savings and infrastructure in South Korea and China; some open economies did not grow. Conclusion: Globalisation provided opportunities, but domestic policies determined which countries could take advantage.
